common_name: Pugster Amethyst Butterfly Bush (Dwarf True-Purple Compact Buddleja)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; cut back hard in late winter to encourage vigorous, floriferous new growth on this dwarf, thick-stemmed selection.

directions: Pugster Amethyst is part of the dwarf Pugster butterfly bush series, bred for unusually thick, sturdy stems and large flower spikes on a plant that stays under two feet tall, a striking contrast to the tall, willowy growth of standard Buddleja davidii. It produces true purple-amethyst flowers continuously from early summer through frost, drawing butterflies and hummingbirds just as reliably as full-size cultivars despite its diminutive stature, and its low, dense habit fits containers, small borders, and mass plantings where larger butterfly bush would overwhelm the space. Like other modern Buddleja hybrids it is sterile and does not self-seed, and it needs only an annual hard cutback in late winter to stay compact and free-flowering.

common_name: Pugster Pink Butterfly Bush (Dwarf Compact Pink Buddleja)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; cut back hard in late winter to encourage vigorous, floriferous new growth on this dwarf, thick-stemmed selection.

directions: Pugster Pink shares the same thick-stemmed, dwarf habit as the rest of the Pugster butterfly bush series, staying under two feet tall while still carrying large, dense flower spikes in a clear rose-pink, blooming continuously from early summer through frost. The compact, sturdy form fits small borders, containers, and foundation plantings where standard butterfly bush cultivars grow far too large, and it draws butterflies and hummingbirds with the same intensity as full-size cultivars. It is sterile and does not self-seed like older Buddleja davidii selections, and needs only an annual hard cutback in late winter, to about 6-12 inches, to stay dense and floriferous.

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained to moist soil in full sun to partial shade; Tiny Wine's compact size fits foundation plantings and small borders where larger ninebark cultivars like Diabolo would quickly outgrow the space.

directions: Tiny Wine is a compact ninebark selection carrying the same deep wine-red to purple maple-like foliage as larger dark-leaved cultivars but on a rounded shrub roughly half the size, staying well under 5 feet tall and wide. Clusters of small white-to-pink spring flowers draw pollinators and are followed by reddish seed capsules, while the exfoliating bark provides winter interest once the leaves drop. Like other ninebarks it tolerates a very wide range of soil conditions, including clay and periodic flooding, and full sun brings out the darkest, richest foliage color; renewal-prune by removing some of the oldest stems at the base every few years to keep the plant full and vigorous.

common_name: Center Glow Ninebark (Glowing Bicolor Foliage Ninebark)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained to moist soil in full sun to partial shade; Center Glow's two-tone leaf coloring is most vivid in full sun and fades toward a more uniform green-purple in shadier spots.

directions: Center Glow is a large, vigorous ninebark selected for unusual bicolor foliage: new leaves emerge with wine-purple margins surrounding a glowing chartreuse-to-orange center, an effect most pronounced on fresh spring and summer growth before the whole leaf gradually deepens toward purple with age, giving the shrub a constantly shifting, luminous look through the season. Clusters of small white-to-pink flowers in late spring draw pollinators, followed by reddish seed capsules and, once leaves drop, attractive exfoliating bark for winter interest. Like other ninebarks it is exceptionally tolerant of clay, poor soil, drought, and periodic flooding, and needs only occasional renewal pruning of the oldest stems at the base to stay full and vigorous.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; foliage color and bloom are both best with at least six hours of direct sun, and Midnight Wine's very low, spreading habit suits it to edging and small-space plantings.

directions: Midnight Wine was the original dwarf dark-leaved weigela that later inspired the even smaller Fine Wine, staying under 18 inches tall and wide with dense, deep burgundy-purple foliage that holds its color through the growing season. Clusters of rose-pink, trumpet-shaped flowers appear in a heavy late-spring flush that draws hummingbirds, and the low, spreading, mounded habit works well as a border edge, small-space accent, or mixed container planting where taller weigela cultivars would be out of scale. It is drought-tolerant and largely trouble-free once established, needing only a light shaping right after the main spring bloom and an occasional renewal cut to the oldest wood to keep growth vigorous.
sources: Proven Winners — Midnight Wine weigela notes
